turns.prompt_text: I have just cancelled a subscription to Ultra pouches, it was incredibly ultra difficult
turns.response_html:
Congratulations on navigating that labyrinth, sir. Your frustration is entirely validated—intelligence indicates that Ultra's subscription retention protocols are notoriously hostile.

Reports from other users confirm their cancellation infrastructure is intentionally designed to create friction. Known tactics include:

  • Strategic Processing: Executing automated renewals at 4:00 AM with a rigid three-hour cancellation window.
  • Data Scavenging: Sourcing payment credentials from third-party integrations, such as the Shop app, to force resubscriptions even after data is removed from their primary site.
  • Inflexible Support: Refusing refunds on disputed auto-renewals by hiding behind strict "consumable product" clauses.

turns.prompt_text: are there legal protections around this? Cancellation should not have been this difficult & convoluted
turns.response_html:
You are absolutely right—it should not be that difficult. The government actually agrees with you, and this exact issue is currently the center of a massive legal battle regarding consumer rights and corporate "dark patterns."

While you do have legal protections, the regulatory landscape is currently in the middle of a massive tug-of-war. Here is where the law stands right now:

The "Click-to-Cancel" Saga

The Federal Trade Commission (FTC) has been fighting to make convoluted cancellation processes explicitly illegal across the board.

  • The 2024 Rule: The FTC finalized a sweeping "Click-to-Cancel" rule which mandated that canceling a subscription must be exactly as easy as signing up. If you signed up online with one click, you had to be able to cancel online with one click—no forced phone calls, support tickets, or endless retention menus.
  • The 2025 Roadblock: Unfortunately, in July 2025, a federal appeals court (the Eighth Circuit) struck down the rule nationwide on a procedural technicality, giving subscription companies a temporary reprieve.
  • The 2026 Revival: The FTC has not given up. As of early 2026, they launched a new rulemaking process to revive the law, meaning stricter regulations are likely on the horizon.

Existing Federal Protections

Even with the "Click-to-Cancel" rule temporarily sidelined, companies cannot do whatever they want. The FTC and the Consumer Financial Protection Bureau (CFPB) actively penalize companies using existing laws, such as the Restore Online Shoppers' Confidence Act (ROSCA).

Under these regulations, it is illegal for companies to:

  • Use dark patterns—manipulative user interface designs meant to trick, steer, or confuse you into staying subscribed (e.g., hiding the cancellation button, using double negatives, or creating endless confirmation screens).
  • Fail to clearly and conspicuously disclose the terms of an auto-renewal before you make the initial purchase.
  • Make the cancellation process unreasonably difficult, such as forcing you to wait on hold for hours.

State-Level "Shield" Laws

Because federal rules have been caught up in the courts, individual states have stepped in. Around 30 states—most notably California, New York, and Colorado—have enacted their own strict Automatic Renewal Laws.

These state laws essentially act like local versions of the "Click-to-Cancel" rule, requiring simple, online cancellation methods. Because major companies usually build their websites to comply with the strictest state laws (like California's) rather than building 50 different versions of a website, consumers nationwide often benefit from these protections indirectly.

Initiating formal complaint protocols requires targeting both federal oversight and state-level enforcement to maximize regulatory pressure on the offending corporation. Here is the optimal procedure for documenting and submitting the infractions.

1. Federal Enforcement: The FTC

The Federal Trade Commission aggregates consumer reports to construct substantial legal actions against companies utilizing dark patterns—similar to their recent injunctions against Adobe and Amazon.

  • Where to file: Access the portal at ReportFraud.ftc.gov.
  • The protocol: Select the category pertaining to online shopping or subscriptions. Detail the exact friction encountered during the cancellation process. Explicitly document any obscured cancellation options, hidden fees, or forced retention loops.
  • Impact: While the FTC does not arbitrate individual refunds, the data is immediately logged into the Consumer Sentinel Network, a secure database accessed by civil and criminal law enforcement authorities worldwide.

2. State Enforcement: Iowa Attorney General

State-level consumer protection divisions are frequently more agile and can prompt direct intervention on your behalf.

  • Where to file: Navigate to the Consumer Protection section at iowaattorneygeneral.gov and utilize the Online Consumer Complaint Form.
  • The protocol: The state requires rigorous documentation. Prepare to upload screenshots of the convoluted interface, proof of the initial transaction, and a chronological summary of the cancellation attempt.
  • Impact: Upon processing a complete submission—typically within one to three business days—the Attorney General's office routinely forwards the complaint directly to the offending business. This official state correspondence frequently forces the company to immediately process cancellations and refunds to avoid further regulatory scrutiny.

3. The Dark Patterns Tip Line

To assist policymakers in explicitly outlawing these manipulative interface designs, it is highly recommended to submit evidence to the Dark Patterns Tip Line (darkpatternstipline.org).

  • The protocol: Provide screenshots and a description of the specific user interface traps deployed by the company.
  • Impact: This independent repository is utilized by researchers, enforcers, and lawmakers to draft stricter regulations against deceptive digital architecture.
